questions.q: What does the + operator do when used between two text fields in a Tableau calculation?
options: Compares them for equality
Causes a syntax error, since + only works on numbers
Adds their character counts together as a number
Concatenates them into one combined string
questions.explain: When both sides are text, + performs string concatenation — joining the two strings together, as in [First Name] + " " + [Last Name].

Everything except the first 4 characters
The first 4 characters of the Order ID string
The 4th character only
questions.explain: LEFT(string, num_chars) returns the first num_chars characters — here, the first 4 characters of Order ID.

options: The position where "Furniture" starts inside Category
A TRUE/FALSE value depending on whether "Furniture" appears anywhere in Category
The number of times "Furniture" appears in Category
A new string with "Furniture" removed from Category
questions.explain: CONTAINS returns a Boolean — TRUE if the substring appears anywhere in the string, FALSE otherwise — which is why it's commonly used inside IF statements.

questions.q: What is the difference between CONTAINS and REPLACE?
options: CONTAINS only works on numbers, REPLACE only works on text
They do the same thing, just with different argument order
REPLACE checks existence, CONTAINS performs the substitution
CONTAINS checks whether a substring exists and returns TRUE/FALSE; REPLACE actually swaps a substring for another string
questions.explain: CONTAINS is a yes/no test for whether a substring is present; REPLACE actually performs the substitution, swapping the found substring for a replacement.

questions.q: Why might you write TRIM(UPPER([Category])) instead of just [Category]?
options: To convert the field from a Dimension into a Measure
Because TRIM and UPPER are required syntax for every string field
To normalize inconsistent real-world text data — forcing consistent capitalization and removing stray leading/trailing whitespace
Because [Category] alone would cause a syntax error
questions.explain: Real data is often inconsistent — the same category might appear as "Furniture", "furniture", or "FURNITURE " with trailing spaces — and wrapping UPPER inside TRIM normalizes both capitalization and whitespace.
